meta_description: Decentralized identity that works offline: governed issuers, wallets people keep, 150–260ms verification and a trust charter that prevents issuer lock-in and cold-start failure.

blocks.x: DIDs and verifiable credentials that work offline: issuers governed by charter, holder wallets people keep using, selective disclosure that shares less, and revocation that actually propagates in minutes — verification in 210ms, without a phone call.
Wallet adoption lives or dies at the consumer-app intersection
blocks.sub: Cold-start economics, one-scan verification and privacy-by-protocol design

blocks.x: Decentralized identity earns its keep when verification works without calling home: a credential presented offline, checked against cryptographic proofs, with selective disclosure so the holder shares the attribute and not the whole file. The engineering is the trust triangle done properly — issuer governance, holder experience, verifier SDKs.
The practice spans DID method selection, credential schemas, issuance workflows (with revocation that actually works), wallet integration, and the verifier side where latency and evidence matter.
Below: the failure modes that strand credential ecosystems, the reference architecture of the trust triangle, and the console that keeps verification fast and revocation real.
Issuer lock-in to wallet abandonment: how credential ecosystems strand
blocks.sub: Empty wallets, beaconing queries, slow revocation, unowned trust registries

blocks.x: Each of these kills adoption quietly — the countermeasures treat issuer governance, wallet UX and revocation as engineering deliverables, not roadmap promises.

Adoption is a cold-start problem, not a cryptography problem
blocks.sub: Why the trust triangle lives or dies on issuer economics and verifier convenience

blocks.x: Verifiable-credential ecosystems fail for the reason marketplaces fail: issuers will not issue without verifiers, verifiers will not verify without holders, and holders delete wallets that sit empty. The engineering answer is sequencing, not evangelism — pick the pair with existing economic gravity (an employer issuing to employees who already verify at a gate, a university issuing to students who already verify at a licensure board), ship the verifier SDK to the one-scan standard (a verification must be one action, under five seconds, with the trust registry doing the policy work), and let revocation propagation under ten minutes make the credentials operationally real rather than ceremonial.

Privacy review is the launch gate: selective disclosure, no beaconing to issuers (verifier queries must not leak to the issuer who issued), and retention rules for the status registry that survive DPA scrutiny. The identity console reads adoption honestly — issuance counts, verification counts, wallet retention — because a trust framework that is not being verified is a pilot, no matter how elegant the cryptography.

Why will people actually keep and use the wallet?

The wallet ships inside apps people already use — the employee badge rides the workplace app, the membership proof rides the loyalty app. Adoption is a cold-start problem solved at the consumer-app intersection, not a new app to download.

Credentials carry cryptographic predicates that verify locally: 70–100% of the listed flows verify without a network call, and the console reports the offline-capable share per credential type as a signed design target.

The trust charter governs issuers, and credentials are standard verifiable credentials — a holder’s wallet is portable across issuers, and the charter amendment path is documented for exactly that reason.
How are revoked or expired credentials handled?

Revocation registries are checked at verification wherever the network allows, and predicates carry expiry. The console tracks revocation latency per issuer, so a revoked credential stops verifying on evidence, not on schedule.
What does the trust-framework team inherit?
The charter, the issuer onboarding kit, the verifier gates, the console and the privacy overlay — the ecosystem artifacts, not just code, because the charter is the load-bearing document.
